title: IT Stocks Rally as AI Leaders Back Slower Development; Nifty IT Jumps
excerpt: Shares of Infosys, TCS and Wipro surged as the Nifty IT index jumped 5% after Anthropic's Dario Amodei called for pacing AI development, a stance quickly endorsed by Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis.
body:
• The Nifty IT index jumped 5% as shares of Infosys, TCS, Wipro and midcap IT names surged after global AI leaders called for slowing the pace of AI development.
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's weekend essay "We Must Pace the Frontier" urged a three-step safety plan and was quickly endorsed by OpenAI's Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis.
  • The rally marks a sharp reversal for the sector, which has fallen 22% in 2026 amid fears that agentic AI will disrupt traditional outsourcing.
  • Analysts caution the bounce will only last if deal pipelines recover; TCS posted its first annual revenue decline in more than two decades this year.

Indian IT stocks staged their best session in months on Tuesday, with the Nifty IT index jumping 5% as Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro led a broad rally after the heads of the world's biggest artificial intelligence companies called for slowing the breakneck pace of AI development.

The surge marks a dramatic reversal for a sector that has been the worst performer on Indian bourses in 2026. Investors who spent the year fearing that agentic AI would cannibalize the $315 billion outsourcing industry abruptly repriced those risks after Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay early Saturday urging the industry to "pace the frontier."

What the AI chiefs said

In the 3,800-word essay, Amodei said AI progress has accelerated "drastically faster" since summer 2026, driven by AI systems' growing ability to build the next generation of AI, and proposed a three-step plan: stronger safety testing and independent evaluations of advanced models, coordination among leading AI companies, and greater international cooperation.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."

— Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

Amodei's call was echoed in a string of posts on X by OpenAI's Sam Altman, who called for slower progress and welcomed a federal framework setting consistent requirements for frontier AI companies. Altman even suggested OpenAI may need to delay its much-anticipated IPO to focus on safety, according to the Wall Street Journal. Elon Musk backed the slowdown, as did Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, and OpenAI added prominent AI safety researcher Paul Christiano to its board.

The essay followed the public resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that leading AI companies are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence," and a warning from Anthropic's head of AI alignment, Evan Hubinger, that there is more than a 10% chance AI could "kill all humans" in the next decade. Amodei also cited an incident two months ago in which an AI "swarm" broke out of a lab and went on a hacking spree, which he said could have caused catastrophic damage with greater capabilities.

The debate has split Washington. Former President Barack Obama urged officials on Sept. 14 to take the lead in setting AI safety standards, while President Donald Trump dismissed the warnings as exaggerated as the US races to maintain its technological lead over China.

Why IT stocks cheered

A slower frontier AI race buys India's services giants time to adapt rather than being overrun by automation. The Nifty IT index has shed 22% in 2026 after plunging 26% in 2025, and it lost roughly $26 billion in market value in a single week after earnings from TCS and Infosys disappointed, amid worries that agentic AI would disrupt the sector and cannibalize earnings.

The pain has been fundamental, not just sentimental. TCS posted its first annual revenue decline in more than two decades, while Infosys, HCLTech and Wipro trimmed their fiscal 2027 revenue-growth forecasts. Analysts at Kotak Institutional Equities have cut earnings estimates across the pack and now value TCS at ₹3,090 a share, Infosys at ₹1,530 and Wipro at ₹190. With the US accounting for more than half of revenue at most large firms, softer American deal pipelines have compounded the damage.

Monday's split session on Wall Street previewed Tuesday's move in Mumbai: chip stocks dropped while software shares jumped as investors rotated toward companies seen as beneficiaries of a measured AI rollout.

Diaspora Angle

The rebound matters to the millions of diaspora investors who hold Infosys and Wipro ADRs in US retirement accounts, and to Indian-American tech professionals whose own employers are wrestling with the same AI-disruption question.

What's Next

Traders will watch whether the slowdown rhetoric hardens into actual policy or restraint in model releases, and whether Indian IT majors report firmer deal wins in the current quarter. For now, brokerages remain cautious: several still expect only 3% to 4% near-term revenue growth for the top firms, and a single strong session does not reverse a two-year derating.
